lead.en: Arminius wipes out three legions and Rome halts at the Rhine

summary.en: Germanic tribes led by Arminius ambushed and destroyed three Roman legions under Varus. Rome abandoned the conquest of Germania, and the imperial frontier remained on the Rhine for centuries.

title.en: Wang Mang founds the Xin dynasty

lead.en: A regent toppled the Han to remake China by ancient books

summary.en: In AD 9 the regent Wang Mang deposed the Han and made himself emperor of a new Xin dynasty. He tried to nationalise land, ban the sale of slaves and bring back coinage on ancient models, but the reforms failed and he was killed in an uprising in AD 23.

lead.en: A Yuezhi chief builds an empire astride the Silk Road

summary.en: Around AD 30 Kujula Kadphises united the five Yuezhi tribes settled in Bactria. His successors built an empire from the Amu Darya to the Ganges valley. The Kushans held key stretches of the Silk Road between Rome, Parthia, India and China; Gandharan art flourished, and Buddhism spread into Central Asia and China.

lead.en: The execution of a Galilean preacher gives rise to Christianity

summary.en: Jesus of Nazareth, a preacher from Galilee, was crucified in Jerusalem on the orders of the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, usually dated AD 30 or 33. His followers' belief in his resurrection became the foundation of Christianity.

lead.en: A marble stable, an ivory manger and 18 servants

summary.en: According to Suetonius, Caligula's favourite horse Incitatus had a marble stable and an ivory manger and 'invited' guests to dinner, and the emperor planned to make him consul. Ancient sources are clear that the horse never actually became consul.

lead.en: Two sisters on war elephants defy the Han Empire

summary.en: In 40 AD the sisters Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị rose against the Han governor of Jiaozhi, today's northern Vietnam. Within months the rebels took dozens of towns and Trưng Trắc was proclaimed ruler. In 43 the general Ma Yuan crushed the revolt, but the sisters became the great heroines of Vietnamese history and are still honoured today.

title.en: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

lead.en: A Greek merchant's guide, the first to map East Africa's trade

summary.en: Around the mid-1st century an anonymous Greek merchant from Egypt wrote a guide to the trade routes of the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. He described the port of Adulis, ruled by King Zoskales, and the southernmost market he knew, Rhapta on the coast of today's Tanzania. Ivory, tortoiseshell and rhino horn were shipped from there: East Africa was already part of ocean trade.

lead.en: A steam engine in Alexandria, treated as a toy

summary.en: Hero of Alexandria described a sphere spun by jets of steam escaping from two bent nozzles. It is the first known steam turbine, yet nobody found a use for it, and it was shown off as a curiosity.

lead.en: Nero was out of town, and the fiddle not yet invented

summary.en: In July 64 a fire raged through Rome for six days and destroyed much of the city. According to Tacitus, Nero was away at Antium; on his return he opened the Campus Martius and his own gardens to the homeless.

lead.en: By tradition, the first Buddhist temple in China

summary.en: Tradition says the Han emperor Ming dreamed of a golden deity and sent envoys to the west. They returned with the Indian monks Kāśyapa Mātaṅga and Dharmaratna, who brought sutras on white horses. In 68 a temple was built for them near Luoyang, regarded as the first Buddhist temple in China.

title.en: Siege of Jerusalem and destruction of the Temple

lead.en: Titus burns the Second Temple; Judaism turns to the synagogue

summary.en: During the First Jewish–Roman War, legions under Titus took Jerusalem after a long siege and burned the Second Temple. Its loss transformed Judaism, shifting religious life to the synagogue and the study of the Torah.

lead.en: Emperor Vespasian taxes urine

summary.en: Urine from Rome's public latrines was sold to tanners and fullers, and Vespasian taxed it. When his son Titus objected, the emperor held up a coin and asked whether it smelled. Public urinals in Italy and France are still called vespasiano and vespasienne.

lead.en: Ash buries Pompeii and preserves Roman daily life

summary.en: Vesuvius buried Pompeii, Herculaneum and Stabiae under ash and pyroclastic flows; the scholar Pliny the Elder died in the disaster. The entombed towns preserved a frozen snapshot of everyday Roman life for archaeologists.

lead.en: Named not for its size but for a statue of Nero

summary.en: The Flavian Amphitheatre opened under Titus on the drained lake of Nero's Golden House. Romans called it simply 'the amphitheatre'; the name Colosseum came later, most likely from the colossal bronze statue of Nero that stood beside it.

title.en: Ban Chao, Protector General of the Western Regions

lead.en: A Han general wins back the Silk Road oases for China

summary.en: For almost 30 years General Ban Chao fought and bargained with the city-states of the Tarim Basin, pushing out the Xiongnu. In 91 he was made Protector General of the Western Regions. In 97 he sent the envoy Gan Ying towards the Roman Empire, but Gan Ying got only as far as a sea west of Parthia and turned back.

title.en: Gan Ying turns back from Rome

lead.en: China's envoy to Rome is talked out of it by sailors

summary.en: General Ban Chao sent Gan Ying to Rome. He reached the 'western sea', where Parthian sailors told him the voyage could take two years and travellers carried three years' supplies. He turned back, though the Roman border was only weeks away overland.

lead.en: One of the world's four great powers, said a contemporary

summary.en: From the 1st century AD the kingdom of Aksum in northern Ethiopia controlled Red Sea trade through the port of Adulis. Its kings minted their own gold coins, a rarity in the ancient world, and in the 3rd century the prophet Mani named Aksum one of the four great kingdoms alongside Rome, Persia and China. Its granite stelae, up to 33 m tall, still recall its power.

lead.en: Peru's irrigators raise adobe pyramids and lifelike pottery

summary.en: On Peru's north coast the Moche culture arose, with irrigated farming and monumental adobe pyramids such as the Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna. Moche artisans were famed for realistic portrait ceramics and fine metalwork.

lead.en: A Roman woman invites a friend to her birthday party

summary.en: A Roman fort in northern Britain preserved wooden tablets with letters from officers and their families. The best known is Claudia Severa's invitation to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to a birthday party around AD 100, one of the oldest known texts in Latin by a woman.

title.en: Cai Lun and the invention of paper

lead.en: Cheap pulp from rags and bark replaces bamboo and silk

summary.en: The court eunuch Cai Lun presented the Han emperor with a method of making paper from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets. The cheap, light material replaced bamboo slips and silk, and later spread through the Islamic world to Europe.

lead.en: Still the largest unreinforced concrete dome after 1,900 years

summary.en: The Pantheon, completed under Hadrian, is crowned by a 43-metre concrete dome with an open oculus at the top; its height to the oculus equals its diameter. Almost two thousand years on, it is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

lead.en: The Kushan king carries Buddhism along the Silk Road

summary.en: Kanishka, the greatest Kushan ruler, governed an empire from Central Asia to the Ganges valley from his capital at Purushapura. A patron of Buddhism, he fostered Gandharan art and the spread of the faith along the Silk Road.

lead.en: Bronze dragons show where an earthquake has struck

summary.en: The court astronomer Zhang Heng built the world's first seismoscope, a bronze vessel with eight dragons. When the ground shook, a ball dropped from one dragon's mouth into a toad's, showing the direction. According to the chronicle, in 138 it registered an earthquake in Longxi, some 500 km away, that no one in the capital had felt.

lead.en: The last Jewish war against Rome begins a long exile

summary.en: When Emperor Hadrian decided to rebuild Jerusalem as the Roman colony of Aelia Capitolina, the Jews revolted under Simon bar Kokhba. Rome crushed the revolt after the fall of the fortress of Betar; hundreds of thousands died. Jews were banned from Jerusalem, and the province was renamed Syria Palaestina.

lead.en: A geocentric system that held sway for 1,400 years

summary.en: The Alexandrian scholar Claudius Ptolemy summed up the astronomy of his day in 13 books. In his system the Earth sits motionless at the centre, and the planets' motions are explained by epicycles; a catalogue of over a thousand stars in 48 constellations is included. The name Almagest comes from the Arabic translation, and until Copernicus it remained the standard astronomy textbook.

title.en: Funan and the port of Óc Eo

lead.en: A Roman medallion of Antoninus Pius turned up in the Mekong delta

summary.en: Funan, the earliest known state of Southeast Asia, flourished from the 1st to the 6th century. Its port of Óc Eo linked India and China, trading beads, gold and spices, and archaeologists found a Roman medallion of Antoninus Pius there. Most of what we know of Funan comes from the reports of 3rd-century Chinese envoys.

lead.en: Returning legions bring home a disease that kills millions

summary.en: Legions returning from war in Mesopotamia brought an epidemic into the Roman Empire, described by the physician Galen and most likely smallpox. Over 15 years it killed millions by various estimates, possibly including co-emperor Lucius Verus.

lead.en: A peasant sect shakes the Han and begins the dynasty's end

summary.en: The Daoist preacher Zhang Jue raised hundreds of thousands of peasants with the slogan 'The Blue Heaven is dead; the Yellow Heaven shall rise'. The main rebel forces were crushed within the year, but the generals who put down the revolt gained armies of their own. The Han empire broke up into warlord domains and then the Three Kingdoms.

lead.en: A Cham sea kingdom that would last some 1,500 years

summary.en: According to Chinese chronicles, in 192 a local ruler named Khu Liên broke away from the Han and founded the kingdom of Linyi on the coast of central Vietnam, the future Champa. The Cham people lived by sea trade, practised Hinduism and built brick tower-shrines at Mỹ Sơn. The last remnant of Champa was absorbed by Vietnam only in 1832.

lead.en: The Praetorians sell the throne to the highest bidder

summary.en: After murdering Emperor Pertinax, the Praetorian Guard announced it would sell the throne. The dead man's father-in-law offered each soldier 20,000 sesterces; Didius Julianus, shouting bids over the camp wall, offered 25,000 and won. He was killed 66 days later.

title.en: Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan

lead.en: Teotihuacan grows into the largest city in the Americas

summary.en: Around AD 200 the Pyramid of the Sun, one of the largest structures of the pre-Columbian Americas, was completed. Teotihuacan, with an estimated 100,000 people, became the largest city in the Americas and shaped all of Mesoamerica.

lead.en: The oral law is written down as Judaism outlives the Temple

summary.en: Around 200 in Galilee the patriarch Judah ha-Nasi gathered into one code the oral law that generations of sages had passed on by word of mouth, all the more precious after the destruction of the Temple in 70. The Mishnah's sixty-three tractates cover agriculture, festivals, marriage, courts and ritual purity. It became the basis of both Talmuds, the Jerusalem and the Babylonian, and of all rabbinic Judaism.

lead.en: A clay jar with copper and iron: an ancient battery?

summary.en: A Parthian or Sasanian jar held a copper cylinder and an iron rod, much like a galvanic cell. Replicas filled with vinegar give a fraction of a volt, but no wires were found, and most scholars think it simply stored scrolls.

lead.en: A hundred bronze puzzles nobody can explain

summary.en: More than a hundred hollow bronze twelve-sided objects, with holes of different sizes and knobs on the corners, have turned up in Rome's north-western provinces. No Roman text mentions them, and the guesses range from surveying tool to knitting aid.

title.en: Fall of the Han and the Three Kingdoms

lead.en: Cao Pi ends the Han and China splits into three

summary.en: Cao Pi forced the last Han emperor to abdicate and founded the state of Wei; the rival states of Shu and Wu soon followed. The Three Kingdoms era, later romanticised in Luo Guanzhong's novel, is one of the best-known periods of Chinese history.

lead.en: Ardashir topples Parthia and gives Rome a new rival

summary.en: The Persian ruler Ardashir I defeated the last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, and founded the Sasanian dynasty with its capital at Ctesiphon. With Zoroastrianism as state religion, the new empire was Rome's main rival for four centuries.

lead.en: New Zealand's biggest blast in 20,000 years, and no one saw it

summary.en: Around AD 232 (±10 years) Taupō produced New Zealand's largest eruption in 20,000 years, scorching the land and reshaping its caldera lake. No human saw it: people would not reach these islands for another thousand years.

lead.en: The first ruler of Japan known to us by name

summary.en: In 239 an embassy from Queen Himiko of Yamatai reached the court of the Chinese kingdom of Wei and obtained for her the title 'Queen of Wa, friend of Wei' and a gold seal. The Chinese chronicle describes Himiko as a shaman-priestess who lived in seclusion. Whether Yamatai lay in Kyushu or around Nara is still debated.

lead.en: A mystery disease ravages Rome through a decade of crisis

summary.en: Named after Bishop Cyprian of Carthage, who described it, this epidemic ravaged the Roman Empire for over a decade amid the Crisis of the Third Century. Its cause is unknown; smallpox and a viral haemorrhagic fever are among the suggestions.

title.en: Rise of the Classic Maya cities

lead.en: Pyramid city-states rise in the Petén jungle

summary.en: Around 250 the Classic Maya period begins, as city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul and Copán grow in the Petén jungle. The Maya built stepped pyramids, kept a precise calendar and recorded their rulers' history in hieroglyphic script.

title.en: The tomb of the Lord of Sipán

lead.en: An untouched Moche royal tomb, full of gold and silver

summary.en: Around the 3rd century a Moche ruler was buried in the adobe pyramid of Huaca Rajada with attendants, warriors and a wealth of gold, silver and turquoise ornaments. In 1987 the archaeologist Walter Alva found the tomb untouched by looters, one of the major South American finds of the 20th century. The treasures are kept in the Royal Tombs of Sipán Museum.

title.en: Battle of Edessa: a Roman emperor taken captive

lead.en: For the first time, a Roman emperor is taken captive

summary.en: The Sasanian king Shapur I crushed a Roman army near Edessa and captured Emperor Valerian along with his staff. Valerian died in captivity in Persia. Shapur celebrated the triumph on a rock relief at Naqsh-e Rostam showing the defeated Roman before the mounted king — an unprecedented humiliation for Rome.

lead.en: A desert queen defied Rome and seized half its East

summary.en: After the death of Palmyra's ruler Odaenathus, his widow Zenobia, ruling for their son, took Egypt, Syria and much of Asia Minor. In 272 Emperor Aurelian defeated her army and captured the queen herself. When the city rebelled a year later the Romans sacked it, and the richest caravan city of the desert never recovered.

lead.en: Lava buries an early city and clears the way for Teotihuacan

summary.en: Radiocarbon dates place the Xitle eruption between AD 245 and 315; its lava buried Cuicuilco, one of Mesoamerica's first large cities. The flight of its people seems to have helped the rise of nearby Teotihuacan.

lead.en: Tiridates III makes Christianity the religion of his realm

summary.en: King Tiridates III, converted by Gregory the Illuminator, made Christianity the state religion of Armenia. By the traditional date Armenia became the first Christian state, and the cathedral of Etchmiadzin was founded at Vagharshapat.

lead.en: An emperor abdicates and refuses to come back

summary.en: Diocletian was the first Roman emperor to abdicate voluntarily, retiring to a seaside palace. Begged to return, he replied that if they could see the cabbages he had grown with his own hands, they would never ask. The palace is now half of Split's old town.

lead.en: Nomads take the Jin capital, and northern China falls apart

summary.en: Troops of the Xiongnu-led Han-Zhao state took Luoyang, massacred tens of thousands and carried off Emperor Huai of Jin. For three centuries the north was split among non-Chinese kingdoms, while the Jin court and masses of refugees moved south to Jiankang (Nanjing).

lead.en: Constantine and Licinius end the persecution of Christians

summary.en: Emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed at Mediolanum to grant freedom of worship and restore property seized from Christians. Persecution ended, and with Constantine's patronage Christianity rapidly became the religion of the empire.

lead.en: Chandragupta I opens the golden age of northern India

summary.en: Chandragupta I took the title 'king of kings', founding the Gupta Empire and a new calendar era. Under his successors northern India enjoyed a 'golden age' of Sanskrit literature, mathematics, astronomy and art.

title.en: Pachomius founds the first communal monastery

lead.en: Life under a common rule: the model for monasteries East and West

summary.en: Around 320 Pachomius, a Coptic former Roman soldier, gathered monks at Tabennisi on the Nile who lived not as hermits but as a community, with shared work, meals and a written rule. By his death in 348 he led nine monasteries for men and two for women, with thousands of members. Jerome translated his rule into Latin, and through Basil the Great and Benedict of Nursia communal monasticism spread across the Christian world.

lead.en: Bishops condemn Arianism and adopt the Nicene Creed

summary.en: Summoned by Emperor Constantine, the first ecumenical council of bishops condemned Arianism and adopted the Nicene Creed, declaring the Son of one substance with the Father. It set a precedent for settling church disputes with imperial backing.

lead.en: Constantine moves the capital to the Bosporus for 1,000 years

summary.en: On 11 May 330 Emperor Constantine dedicated a new capital on the site of Greek Byzantium on the Bosporus. Constantinople remained the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire for more than a thousand years.

lead.en: King Ezana puts the cross on Aksum's coins

summary.en: King Ezana of Aksum, guided by his tutor Frumentius, converted to Christianity, and the cross replaced pagan symbols on his coins. Aksum, a trading power linking Rome, Arabia and India, became one of the world's first Christian states.

lead.en: Tradition credits a captive woman preacher, Saint Nino

summary.en: King Mirian III of Kartli and his court converted to Christianity, by various estimates between 326 and 337. Tradition links it to the preaching of Saint Nino, who came from Cappadocia. Georgia became one of the world's first Christian states, and a church was founded at Mtskheta on the site of the later Svetitskhoveli Cathedral.

lead.en: Roman glass that changes colour: 4th-century nanotech

summary.en: In reflected light the cup is green; lit from behind it glows red. The secret is gold and silver particles only tens of nanometres across mixed into the glass, though the Roman makers can hardly have known why it worked.

lead.en: A tsunami tosses Alexandria's ships onto rooftops

summary.en: On 21 July 365 a great earthquake lifted western Crete by several metres, and a tsunami struck coasts from Sicily to Egypt. Ammianus Marcellinus described ships in Alexandria hurled by the wave onto rooftops.

lead.en: A Teotihuacan general reshapes Tikal and its dynasty

summary.en: In January 378 the warlord Siyaj K'ak', linked to Teotihuacan, arrived at the great Maya city of Tikal; the same day its king died. A new ruler was installed, and Tikal went on to dominate the Maya lowlands for centuries.

lead.en: A priest of Isis carved hieroglyphs almost no one could read

summary.en: On 24 August 394 the priest Nesmeterakhem carved an inscription and an image of the god Mandulis in the temple of Isis at Philae. It is the last known dated text in Egyptian hieroglyphs, a script that had to be deciphered from scratch some 1,400 years later.

lead.en: East and West part ways: one falls, the other lasts 1,000 years

summary.en: On the death of Theodosius I, the last emperor to rule the whole empire, it was permanently split between his sons: Arcadius took the East and Honorius the West. The West fell 81 years later, while the East (Byzantium) endured another thousand years.

lead.en: The first great autobiography: a soul gives an account of itself

summary.en: Around 397–400 Augustine, bishop of Hippo in Roman Africa, wrote the Confessions, thirteen books addressed to God. He told of his childhood in Thagaste, a restless youth, his years as a Manichaean and his conversion in Milan in 386, and in the final books reflected on memory and time. The work is considered the first autobiography in Western literature, and its author one of the most influential theologians of Latin Christianity.

lead.en: A monk in his sixties walks from China to India

summary.en: In 399 the Chinese monk Faxian, then about sixty, set out from Chang'an in search of authentic Buddhist scriptures. He crossed the Taklamakan and the Himalayas, studied in India for several years, spent two years in Sri Lanka and returned by sea in 412. His 'Record of Buddhist Kingdoms' is a priceless account of Gupta India.

lead.en: A six-tonne iron pillar that has not rusted in 1,600 years

summary.en: This seven-metre pillar weighing over six tonnes was forged under the Gupta king Chandragupta II. It has barely rusted: its high-phosphorus iron grew a protective film that in 1,600 years has thickened by just one-twentieth of a millimetre.

title.en: Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet

lead.en: A script made for the Bible, still in use 1,600 years on

summary.en: Around 405 the monk Mesrop Mashtots, backed by King Vramshapuh and Catholicos Sahak, devised a 36-letter alphabet. Until then Armenians wrote in Greek and Syriac. His students first translated the Bible, and the 5th century became the “golden age” of Armenian literature. The alphabet is still used, almost unchanged, today.

title.en: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths

lead.en: Alaric sacks Rome, the first foreign capture in 800 years

summary.en: The Visigoths under Alaric captured Rome and plundered it for three days — the first time in almost 800 years that the city fell to a foreign enemy. The shock was immense and moved Augustine to write The City of God.

lead.en: A six-metre chronicle of a Goguryeo king's conquests

summary.en: In 414 King Jangsu raised a stone stele more than six metres high over the tomb of his father, Gwanggaeto the Great. Some 1,800 characters recount the campaigns that made Goguryeo the leading power of Korea and Manchuria. Rediscovered in the 1880s, its passage about the Wa of Japan is still argued over by Korean, Japanese and Chinese historians.

lead.en: A monk lives on top of a pillar for 37 years

summary.en: To escape crowds of pilgrims, the Syrian ascetic Simeon climbed a pillar about 3 m high, then moved to ever taller ones, the last reportedly over 15 m. He lived on a platform of about a square metre for 37 years, preaching to visitors below.

lead.en: An outsider founds a dynasty that ruled for nearly 400 years

summary.en: In 426 Kʼinich Yax Kʼukʼ Moʼ, linked to Teotihuacan and Tikal, took power in Copán. Fifteen more rulers followed, all shown on Altar Q, set up in 776. The founder's tomb was found beneath the Copán acropolis in the 1990s, and analysis of his bones showed he had grown up elsewhere.

lead.en: A university that drew students from all over Asia

summary.en: The Buddhist monastery of Nalanda was founded under the Gupta king Kumaragupta I, around 427 by various estimates. It grew into a vast centre of learning with dormitories, temples and a famous library; Chinese pilgrims report thousands of monks from China, Korea, Tibet and Indonesia living and studying there. Around 1200 Nalanda was sacked by the troops of Bakhtiyar Khalji.

lead.en: Ash smothers the southern Maya lands and empties villages

summary.en: Central America's largest eruption in millennia, dated by Greenland ice cores to AD 429–433. Ash blanketed the southern Maya lands, and settlements for hundreds of kilometres around were temporarily abandoned.

lead.en: Geiseric seizes Rome's richest grain province

summary.en: The Vandals under King Geiseric, who had crossed from Spain into Africa, seized Carthage by surprise. The Western Roman Empire lost its richest grain province, and Carthage became the capital of the Vandal kingdom.

lead.en: Aetius and the Visigoths stop Attila in Gaul

summary.en: The Roman general Aetius, allied with the Visigoths, halted Attila's Hunnic invasion of Gaul; the Visigothic king Theodoric I fell in the battle. It checked the Huns' advance west, and their empire broke up after Attila's death in 453.

lead.en: The 'Scourge of God' dies at his own wedding feast

summary.en: The Hunnic king who terrorised both Roman empires died in 453 after a feast celebrating his marriage to the young Ildico. According to Priscus he suffered a severe haemorrhage, possibly a nosebleed, and choked to death in a drunken stupor.

title.en: The paintings of the Ajanta Caves

lead.en: Masterpieces found by a British officer hunting a tiger

summary.en: About thirty cave monasteries were cut into a cliff above a bend of the Waghora river in two phases; the most famous date to about 460–480 under the Vakataka king Harishena. Their frescoes of the Jatakas, tales of the Buddha's past lives, are the summit of ancient Indian painting. In 1819 a British officer, John Smith, stumbled on the caves while chasing a tiger.

title.en: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

lead.en: Odoacer deposes the last emperor and Antiquity ends

summary.en: The Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. The year is traditionally taken as the end of the Western Roman Empire and the line between antiquity and the Middle Ages.

lead.en: A parricide king builds his palace on top of a rock

summary.en: King Kashyapa I, who seized the throne after killing his father, moved his capital to the top of a sheer rock some 180 metres high. A stairway led up through a gate shaped like a giant lion, whose stone paws survive. Frescoes of half-clad maidens remain on the cliff, and the polished 'mirror wall' bears verses left by visitors over many centuries.

lead.en: Pi to seven decimals, a record for nearly 900 years

summary.en: By inscribing a polygon with 24,576 sides in a circle, the mathematician Zu Chongzhi found that pi lies between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927. Nobody calculated it more precisely for nearly 900 years.

lead.en: The Frankish king turns Catholic, laying a base for France

summary.en: Clovis I, king of the Franks, was baptised at Reims by Bishop Remigius, traditionally around 496. Unlike other Germanic kings, who were Arians, he chose Catholicism, winning the Franks the support of the Gallo-Roman elite and the Church.

lead.en: A young astronomer computes π and says the Earth spins

summary.en: The 23-year-old Indian astronomer Aryabhata composed a treatise on mathematics and astronomy. It uses place-value notation, gives π ≈ 3.1416 and states that the Earth rotates on its axis.
